items.title: Fed’s Waller says central bank may need to ‘shock people’ with half-point rate hike
items.excerpt: Published Wed, Nov 18 2026 7:20 AM EST Updated 2 Hours Ago ... KEY POINTS - The Federal Reserve's Christopher Waller said a half percentage point increase in the central bank's benchmark rate is probably necessary at its December meeting. - Alternatively, the Fed could raise rates by a quarter point and signal another move was coming in January, Waller told CNBC, though this runs contrary to how Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh has preferred to communicate plans. - Inflation is "headed in the wrong direction, and it's spreading out," Waller told CNBC. Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller on Wednesday called for aggressive action against inflation, saying the central bank needs to "shock people" as prices continue to rise more than he expected. In the near term, the policymaker told CNBC in a live interview that a half percentage point increase in the Fed's benchmark rate is probably necessary at the Dec. 8-9 meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee. He said the central bank needs to reverse the three quarter-point reductions from last year and may need to do more. "I'm very, very concerned about inflation. It's kind of headed in the wrong direction, and it's spreading out," Waller told CNBC's Steve Liesman during a " Squawk Box" interview. "If you really want to get it down, you've got to start taking more aggressive actions." "You might need to, like, shock people," he said. Futures prices are fully pricing in a quarter percentage point hike at the FOMC's December meeting. They also are anticipating another move in January, followed by at least one additional increase before the end of 2027, according to the CME Group's FedWatch gauge. Waller said the Fed wouldn't necessarily have to approve a half-point hike in December if it raised rates by a quarter point and signaled another move coming in January. However, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh has been against that kind of forward guidance on grounds that it ties policymakers' hands. "If you're not going to signal this very clearly to markets, you're going in January, my view is then you have to go 50 [basis points] in December to put it in place and get it done," he said. Recent statements from other central bankers indicate a range of opinions, though most agree that more policy tightening is needed to bring down inflation. In a speech Tuesday, St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem suggested as many as four hikes by the spring of 2027. Some Fed officials, including regional Presidents Beth Hammack of Cleveland and Lorie Logan of Dallas, have endorsed more gradual tightening. However, continued inflation above the Fed's 2% target might push officials into a more aggressive stance. The FOMC approved its first interest rate hike in more than three years in September, and then held rates steady at its October meeting. While inflation has continued to run hot since then, other Fed officials seem less eager to drop the policy hammer as heavily as Waller. "I don't think the situation calls for dramatic action," New York Fed President John Williams said Tuesday in a conversation with Axios. "I think what we've been doing over the last past few months is ... working well. We're collecting the data, analyzing it, having the debate and making a decision." The Fed in 2025 approved three rate cuts amid worries over the labor market and the belief that inflation would continue to moderate toward the central bank's 2% goal. However, inflation reignited earlier this year after the strikes the U.S. and Israel launched against Iran in late February. Energy prices spiked while tariff impacts lingered, keeping most inflation readings above 3%. "First of all, you've got to take back the three insurance cuts we put in last year," Waller said. "If the policy rate last summer in 2025 wasn't bringing inflation down, getting back to that isn't going to bring it down. So we may have to go above ... three hikes plus maybe some more to get it to start actually coming back down."

items.title: Waller says on CNBC the Fed needs to get more aggressive in inflation response By Reuters
items.excerpt: Published Nov 18, 2026, 08:52 AM Updated Nov 18, 2026, 08:54 AM ... By Howard Schneider WASHINGTON, Nov 18 (Reuters) - US Federal Reserve governor Christopher Waller said on Wednesday the central bank needs to get more aggressive in its response to inflation that he fears is changing public psychology about prices, and either approve a half-point hike at the December meeting or communicate a faster pace of hikes in 2027. Inflation is "heading in the wrong direction and it is spreading out," Waller said on CNBC, noting that many of the items with faster-rising prices now are in the services sector and largely beyond the influence of high oil costs and other temporary factors. "If you really want to get it down you’ve got to start taking aggressive actions," either through a larger half-point increase at the coming December 8-9 meeting, or using the post-meeting statement or Chairman Kevin Warsh’s press conference to set market expectations for further hikes. Recent inflation has been running in excess of 3% on an annualized basis and may be accelerating, Waller said, and he fears that business leaders are coming to treat that level as normal and what should be passed through to consumers. "You are starting to hear some of that — ’we put through 3% because we think we can get it’ — and that’s when you start having problems trying to get inflation down," Waller said. "So you might need to shock people to say, wait a minute, 3% is not the number you should be thinking about going forward ... That’s the kind of psychology we need to start breaking ... We can’t wait. We can’t do this in like the next two years." Recent inflation data exceeded a benchmark Waller said he felt would warrant a half-point rate hike at the Fed’s next meeting. He said he felt the choice now was between taking that action, and upending market expectations for only a quarter point hike, or saying very clearly that the Fed would also raise rates again in January and continue higher from there. That could be done in the Fed’s post-meeting statement, or "the chair could actually talk about it ... in the press conference. But we’ve got to do something," Waller said, otherwise "then you have to go 50 in December. Put it in place and get it done." "It’s just starting to spread around and people are starting to accept it more than we want them to," Waller said. Warsh has said he wants to avoid "forward guidance" as much as possible, but Waller said he felt this was a moment when the central bank needed to use strong communications to its benefit and help keep inflation psychology in check. "The Chair has his way of wanting to communicate. That’s fine. Those are his preferences," Waller said. "I’ve been in this game a long time ... You want to use communications as one of your tools ... We should be using communication to do what we want, to get the markets to help us do our job." The Fed held its policy rate steady in October in a range of from 3.75% to 4%. Minutes of that session will be released today at 2pm EDT and provide more detail on the debate.

items.title: Dollar holds near 19-month high as data supports case for rate hikes
items.excerpt: The dollar strengthened to a fresh 19-month high on Wednesday as hawkish commentary from influential US Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller ​and recent economic data cemented expectations for ​an interest rate hike next month. Fed Chair ​Kevin Warsh's refusal to offer forward guidance has made investors more dependent on economic data and commentary from other policymakers to gauge the Fed's next move. Waller said on CNBC that if the central bank wants to get inflation down it needs to take more "aggressive ⁠action" ‌either through a half-point increase at the December meeting, or using the post-meeting ⁠statement to set market expectations for further hikes. Hotter-than-expected inflation data last week have left markets fully pricing a 25-basis-point rate hike in December, and seeing a small chance of a 50-bp rise, the CME Group's FedWatch Tool showed. Data on Tuesday showed US retail sales increased moderately in October, reinforcing expectations for a rate ‌hike next month.

items.title: U.S. Firms’ Year-Ahead Inflation Expectations Rise to 2.5% in November | TokenPost
items.excerpt: By John Kim Published Nov 18, 2026, 10:48 AM EST ... U.S. businesses’ expectations for inflation over the coming year rose to 2.5% in November, while a separate measure of expected unit costs remained above its prepandemic average. The year-ahead business inflation expectation increased from 2.3% in October, a rise of 0.2 percentage point. The unit-cost measure stayed above its 2.0% prepandemic average. The 2.5% reading is for business inflation expectations; the 2.0% figure is the prepandemic average for unit-cost expectations. The November results were released Wednesday, Nov. 18.

items.title: Jeff Bezos was 'heavily involved' in Robert Pattinson's casting as Bond
items.excerpt: Jeff Bezos has said he was "heavily involved" in casting Robert Pattinson as the new James Bond. Speaking at an event in California, the Amazon chairman said he was originally "biased against" Pattinson - who starred in many blockbuster films like Batman and the Twilight series - "because he's already so famous". The role of 007 has typically gone to an actor who is not as well known at the time of casting. But Bezos said in screen tests, "it was so obvious he is James Bond". This will be the first 007 film in the official series not under the creative control of the Broccoli family, who had overseen the franchise since the first movie in 1962. Amazon purchased MGM, which co-owns the franchise, in 2022. "There was something special about Rob", Bezos said at Semafor Silicon Valley & The World Event on Tuesday. Pattinson was unveiled as the franchise's seventh James Bond on Monday, taking over from actor Daniel Craig. He will star in the 26th Bond movie, due to be released in 2028. In a statement, the London-born actor said: "James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime." The next Bond film will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, but its title and exact release date have not yet been announced.
